title: Lindsey Graham's legacy on the ballot: a shelved bribery probe, the Iran war, and his sister's race
dek: ProPublica says an FBI inquiry centered on Graham's $40,000 steak dinner stalled after the bureau's purge. He also helped talk Trump into war with Iran. On Tuesday, voters decide whether his sister keeps his seat.
body:
Two days before South Carolina chooses a senator for the first time since Lindsey Graham’s death, his record is back in the news twice over. In October, ProPublica reported that Graham’s 2020 steakhouse dinner with a defense contractor sat at the center of an FBI bribery inquiry that stalled after the Trump administration’s purge of the bureau [1][2]. Through 2026, Graham was also the leading voice in Congress urging the war with Iran, and he said so publicly [5][7]. His sister, Sen. Darline Graham, now holds his seat and is on Tuesday’s ballot [12][14]. This report looks at the story four ways: the allegations, the war, the race, and the strongest argument each side makes about Iran.

## 1. The $40,000 dinner at the center of a shelved FBI probe

On March 3, 2020, Graham sat down for 45 minutes in a private room at Charlie Palmer Steak in Washington. Across the table were two executives and a lobbyist from Navatek, a small naval contractor based in Hawaii. According to ProPublica, the meeting itself cost $40,000 in pledged campaign contributions [1].

Navatek’s chief executive, Martin Kao, later told the FBI that Graham agreed that night to steer a contract worth about $10 million to the company in South Carolina. In return, Kao said, Graham asked for $100,000 in total pledges to his reelection campaign [1][4]. Graham’s office later added $9.5 million to the budget for the research. It says the money came at the request of Navatek and the University of South Carolina, and was not tied to donations [4].

**Both parties named.** Kao told agents the arrangement was not limited to Republicans. He said Rep. James Clyburn, the state’s senior Democrat, asked how much Navatek was giving Graham and asked for the same amount [2]. Clyburn’s office confirmed that a dinner took place but did not address what was discussed. Rep. Joe Wilson’s dealings with the company were also under review [4].

**The probe that stopped.** Kao was indicted in 2022 for funnelling illegal donations through a shell company, and he cooperated with investigators before going to prison [2]. By early 2025, agents had opened a wider bribery inquiry with the Graham dinner at its center. ProPublica reports that the work stalled after the purge of FBI personnel [1][2]. Nobody was charged.

**The denial.** Graham died suddenly in July at 71. His former spokeswoman, who now works for his sister, called the allegations “simply false.” She said the FBI never contacted the office, that Graham later rejected the donations in question, and that Kao is a convicted felon who would say anything to help himself [3].

**Who benefited.** The contract outlived Navatek. It went to Integer Technologies, a firm founded by two former Navatek executives after Kao’s arrest, one of whom attended the dinner [1]. The Graham story is the second in a ProPublica series that began in September with Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, who also denies wrongdoing [2].

## 2. The senator who sold a war

The United States and Israel struck Iran on February 28, 2026. By Graham’s own account, the road there ran through the golf course. He told Politico that after the 2024 election he spent rounds with Trump pressing the case for confronting Tehran [5]. He pitched regime change as a legacy moment on the scale of the Berlin Wall’s fall and a path to expanding the Abraham Accords [6].

**The inside game.** The Wall Street Journal reported that Graham met Israeli intelligence officials several times in the weeks before the strikes and advised Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on how to make the case to Trump [7]. A White House insider told Politico that Graham had outsized influence on the decision. Graham summed up the president as “a hard sell, but when you sell him, he’s all in” [5].

**The arc of the war.** Graham was the war’s loudest backer on cable news. A month in, he urged Trump to wind the fighting down and pursue a peace deal [22]. By May, with talks stalled, he was floating new strikes on Iran’s “war machine” [9]. Critics noted that his stated measure of victory, a reopened Strait of Hormuz, would restore conditions that existed before the war began [10].

**The political bet.** Graham filed for a fifth term in March and tied his campaign to the war [8]. On NBC he said confronting Iran was worth losing his job, and pressed for more pressure on Tehran [11][19]. Eulogizing him in July, Trump said his friend “never saw a war that he didn’t like” [11].

Graham died on July 11 with the war unresolved. Supporters credit him with forcing a reckoning with a regime they saw as nearing a bomb. Critics, including some on the MAGA right, see a senator who talked a reluctant president into the kind of war he had campaigned against [20]. What neither side disputes is the role Graham claimed for himself.

## 3. A sister inherits the seat, and the war

Two days after Graham’s death, Gov. Henry McMaster appointed his sister, Darline Graham, to finish his term, with Trump’s public backing [12]. She had never held office. Graham became her guardian when she was 13, after their parents died, and later adopted her so she could receive his military benefits [12].

**From placeholder to candidate.** McMaster’s camp reportedly never expected her to run; at Trump’s urging, she did [14]. She led a 10-way special primary on August 11 with about 33 percent and beat Rep. Ralph Norman in the August 25 runoff with about 52 percent, helped by MAGA Inc. money and endorsements from Sen. Tim Scott and McMaster [13][14][15].

**The Iran problem.** Her first ad covered abortion, immigration and girls’ sports, and skipped Iran entirely [11]. In a runoff debate, asked about Taiwan, she said national security was “not my thing” [14]. At the October 11 general-election debate, Democrat Annie Andrews said Graham had three chances to vote to end the war and voted to continue it each time [16][23]. Graham defended the war’s premise, argued that Democrats had let Iran come close to a weapon, and pointed to a sanctions bill she sponsored as a way to end the war economically [17].

**The bribery shadow.** ProPublica’s report on her brother landed in late October. Her office, staffed by his former team, has called the allegations false and the timing unfair to a man who cannot respond [3].

**The math.** Trump carried South Carolina by 18 points in 2024, and no Democrat has won statewide there in two decades [14][18]. A Rasmussen poll taken October 5 to 8 had Graham ahead 49 percent to 45 percent, closer than many expected [18]. Libertarian Kasie Whitener is also on the ballot. Whoever wins, South Carolina will send its first woman to the Senate [18].

## 4. Was Graham right about Iran? Two cases

Here is the strongest version of each argument, as its own advocates make it.

**The case his allies make.** To Graham’s defenders, the war was overdue, not reckless. Iran had spent decades arming Hezbollah and other proxies, and they argue the 2025 strikes on its nuclear sites only delayed a program Tehran meant to rebuild [5]. In this view, a regime closing in on a bomb would have been far more dangerous to confront later. They also see a strategic prize: Graham argued that a weakened Iran would let Israel and the Arab states normalize relations under a Senate-ratified treaty [6]. Pressure, not diplomacy alone, moves Tehran, they say, and stalled talks prove it [19]. Darline Graham’s sanctions bill fits that logic [17].

**The case his critics make.** Restrainers on the left and on the MAGA right say Graham talked a president who ran against forever wars into exactly that [20]. They note the war began without authorization from Congress, has cost American and Iranian lives [24], and has disrupted energy markets through the Strait of Hormuz [10]. They point to a moving target: a call to wind down in March, new strikes floated in May, and a definition of victory that returns to the prewar status quo [9][10][22]. Gulf allies largely stayed on the sidelines, Graham himself complained [21], and veterans’ groups opposing his sister warn of another 20-year commitment [23].

**Where the evidence is contested.** How close Iran was to a weapon before February remains disputed, as does whether the strikes set its program back further than the 2025 attacks did. Whether economic pressure or military force ends the war is a question South Carolina’s voters, and the Senate, will keep answering after Tuesday.
